Welcome. This unit opens the course with a concrete, hands-on
problem — a Brisbane River surge propagating into Moreton Bay — that
threads together every theme you will revisit over the next nine
units: PDEs, Julia, computation, real measurements, the inverse
problem, ocean / water modelling, and PINNs. Then it previews the
larger AIMS thermistor-chain capstone that we close the course with.

## 1.1 A scientific question, in your back yard

### Where the Brisbane River meets Moreton Bay

Most of Brisbane's storm runoff and a meaningful slice of South-East
Queensland's wastewater eventually drains down the **Brisbane
River** and exits at Pile Light into **Moreton Bay** — a shallow,
semi-enclosed body of water bounded by the mainland to the west,
Moreton Island to the east, and North Stradbroke Island to the
south-east. The bay is also a Ramsar-listed estuarine nursery and a
recreational fishery, so what comes down the river matters to
ecology, public health, and shipping.

After heavy rain in the upper catchment, the river runs hard for a
day or two and pushes a *freshwater surge* — a low-density plume
carrying sediment, nutrients, and (occasionally) sewage overflow —
out into the bay. The bay responds: tide gauges across the bay
record a small, transient surface-elevation anomaly riding on top of
the usual tide, even though the wind is calm.

### What we actually measure, and what we don't

Here is the operational catch: the bay has **plenty of tide gauges**
(at the Brisbane Bar, Wellington Point, Tangalooma anchorage, around
the Russell / Macleay channel), but the river outflow itself is hard
to instrument in flood conditions — current meters are washed out,
banks are inaccessible, suspended-sediment loads kill optical
probes. We rarely have a reliable time-history of *what came out of
the river*, only of *how the bay responded*.

That sets up the scientific question we will solve in this unit:

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Unit 1 question
Given **sparse, noisy tide-gauge timeseries** scattered across
Moreton Bay, can we **reconstruct the time-history of the surge at
the river mouth** that produced them?

If we can, the same machinery — a forward physical model plus a
learned source — lets us infer contaminant load, freshwater
discharge, and bay-flushing timescales from measurements that are
already routinely collected.
:::

The same shape of question recurs throughout coastal oceanography:
*given downstream observations, infer the upstream forcing.* It is a
classical **inverse problem**, and we will solve it twice — once
with a naive PINN and once by using the simulator as a forward
operator — so that the failure of the naive approach motivates
everything in Units 5–9.

## 1.2 The worked example

### The geography, made tractable

![Two-panel site map. (a) The SWE-modelling domain (blue rectangle) covers
50 km east–west by 95 km north–south, including the mainland coast,
Moreton Island, North Stradbroke, and the open ocean to the east of
Moreton. The four tide-gauge sites (gold) sit at plausible real
locations across the bay. The red triangle near the western coast is
the **Brisbane River mouth**, where the unknown surge ψ(t) is
imposed. (b) Inset zoom on the river entrance / Pile Light area
where G1 sits, just downstream of where ψ(t) drives the
bay.](figures/site_map.png)

We choose a domain that is small enough to evaluate in seconds on a
laptop but big enough to capture the geography that matters:

- A $50 \times 95\,\text{km}$ rectangle at $1\,\text{km}$
  resolution — so the SWE mesh is $50 \times 95 = 4750$ cells, of
  which about half are water.
- A **hand-built bathymetry** that echoes the real bay: a
  $\sim 6\,\text{m}$ inner-bay flat, an eastern deep channel
  (the NE channel) rising to $\sim 25\,\text{m}$ between Moreton
  Island and the mainland, the dredged $\sim 14\,\text{m}$ Brisbane
  River shipping channel, and a $30$–$50\,\text{m}$ shelf east of
  Moreton Island.
- A **land mask** for the mainland coast, Moreton Island, North
  Stradbroke Island, and a small Peel/Mud cluster mid-bay.

This is not a bathymetric chart — for real work, students should
use AusBathyTopo (Geoscience Australia) or GEBCO global grids. It is
the smallest model that lets the *shape of the answer* be the right
shape.

The bay model is produced by `units/unit_01/scripts/build_bay.jl`
and stored as plain CSVs in `units/unit_01/data/`:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
using DelimitedFiles, CSV, DataFrames
H_grid = readdlm("units/unit_01/data/bay_bathymetry.csv", ',', Float64)
mask   = readdlm("units/unit_01/data/bay_mask.csv",       ',', Int)
gauges = CSV.read("units/unit_01/data/bay_gauges.csv",   DataFrame)
river  = CSV.read("units/unit_01/data/river_source.csv", DataFrame)
```

### The physics in one paragraph

The water motion is described by the **linearised shallow-water
equations** (de Wolff et al. (2021) eq. 6–7; reproduced in detail in
[§7.2](../unit_07/unit_07.qmd#sec-de-wolff)). With $H(x,y)$ the depth
and $g$ gravity, the surface elevation $\eta(x, y, t)$ and depth-
averaged velocity $\mathbf{u}(x, y, t)$ satisfy

$$
\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial t} + \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(H\,\mathbf{u}\bigr) = 0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + g\,\nabla \eta = -b\,\mathbf{u},
$$ {#eq-swe-linear}

with linear drag $b$. Eliminating $\mathbf{u}$ between the two
equations gives a single 2-D wave equation for $\eta$:

$$
\frac{\partial^2 \eta}{\partial t^2}
\;=\; \nabla\!\cdot\!\bigl(g\,H\,\nabla \eta\bigr).
$$ {#eq-wave-eta}

This is the cleanest form to think about and is what the inverse
solver below will use as its physics constraint.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why "linearised"?
We have dropped the Coriolis, advective ($\mathbf{u}\!\cdot\!\nabla\mathbf{u}$),
and Reynolds-stress terms from the full SWE. For surge events of a
few hours over a region $\lesssim 100\,\text{km}$, the dominant
balance is between pressure gradient and free-surface acceleration —
the same balance that gives a tidal wave its speed
$c = \sqrt{g\,H}$. Units 7–8 walk through which terms matter when.
:::

We close the system with a **Dirichlet boundary condition at the
river-mouth cell**:

$$
\eta(x_r, y_r, t) \;=\; \psi(t),
$$

where $\psi(t)$ is the surface-elevation anomaly at the source. In
the forward problem we *prescribe* $\psi(t)$; in the inverse problem
we will *recover* it from gauge data. Solid coasts get $\mathbf{u}
\cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = 0$, and a thin Rayleigh-damped sponge along
the eastern edge of the domain lets surge waves leave through the
open ocean.

### A synthetic surge, propagated by finite differences

To generate the data we will work with, we run the linearised SWE
forward on a staggered Arakawa-C grid with explicit time stepping at
$\Delta t = 12\,\text{s}$ for 6 hours. The "ground-truth" surge is a
two-pulse profile

$$
\psi_{\text{truth}}(t) \;=\;
0.45 \exp\!\left[-\left(\tfrac{t - 2.0\,\text{h}}{0.55\,\text{h}}\right)^2\right]
\;+\;
0.18 \exp\!\left[-\left(\tfrac{t - 4.3\,\text{h}}{0.55\,\text{h}}\right)^2\right]
$$

— a $\sim 45\,\text{cm}$ leading freshwater pulse from heavy
catchment rain, followed by a $\sim 18\,\text{cm}$ follow-on bulge
about two hours later. These amplitudes are realistic for moderate
Brisbane-flood de-tided residuals.

The full forward solve lives in
`units/unit_01/scripts/generate_surge_data.jl`; its inner loop is
just the staggered-grid update:

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# Inner FD step (linearised SWE on an Arakawa-C grid).
for step in 1:NT
    t = step * DT

    # 1. Mass:  ∂η/∂t = -∂(Hu·u)/∂x - ∂(Hv·v)/∂y
    @inbounds for j in 2:NY-1, i in 2:NX-1
        mask[j, i] == 1 || continue
        flux_x_e = Hu[j, i  ] * u[j, i  ]
        flux_x_w = Hu[j, i-1] * u[j, i-1]
        flux_y_n = Hv[j,   i] * v[j,   i]
        flux_y_s = Hv[j-1, i] * v[j-1, i]
        η[j, i] -= DT * ((flux_x_e - flux_x_w) / DX +
                         (flux_y_n - flux_y_s) / DY)
    end

    # 2. Sponge layer absorbs outgoing waves at the east edge
    @inbounds for j in 1:NY, i in 1:NX
        sponge[j, i] > 0 && (η[j, i] -= DT * sponge[j, i] * η[j, i])
    end

    # 3. Apply the river-mouth source (Dirichlet on η at the source cell)
    η[JR, IR] = ψ_truth(t)

    # 4. Momentum (using the new η):  ∂u/∂t = -g ∂η/∂x - b·u
    @inbounds for j in 1:NY, i in 1:NX-1
        if u_open[j, i]
            dηdx = (η[j, i+1] - η[j, i]) / DX
            u[j, i] += DT * (-G_GRAV * dηdx - B_DRAG * u[j, i])
        else
            u[j, i] = 0.0
        end
    end
    # ... v update mirrors u, omitted for brevity ...
end
```

The full grid solve runs in $\sim 3.5\,\text{s}$.

### Watching the surge cross the bay

![Linearised-SWE forward solve: free-surface anomaly η(x,y,t) propagating
outward from the Brisbane River mouth (red triangle) into Moreton Bay.
Gold circles are the four tide-gauge sites. Grey is land — Moreton
Island on the east edge, mainland on the west, North Stradbroke in
the SE, a Peel/Mud island cluster mid-bay. Note how the wave fans
out, gets channeled along the eastern deep trough, reflects off
Moreton Island, and reaches the southern gauges (G4) about half an
hour later than the central ones (G2). Total simulated window: 6 h
at 5-minute frames.](figures/surge_animation.gif)

The animation makes a few points concrete:

1. **Wave speed depends on depth.** $c = \sqrt{g\,H} \approx
   8\,\text{m/s}$ in the inner bay ($H \approx 6\,\text{m}$);
   noticeably faster along the eastern trough.
2. **Geometry matters.** The wave wraps around the Peel/Mud
   island cluster and reflects off Moreton Island.
3. **Different gauges see different signals.** G1 (Brisbane Bar)
   responds first and strongest. G4 (Russell Channel) is the slowest
   and most attenuated. This *information geometry* is what will
   make the inverse problem solvable.

### The measurements we get

The four gauges produce timeseries $\eta_g(t_k)$ at one-minute
sampling. We add $\sigma = 1.5\,\text{cm}$ Gaussian observation
noise to imitate real de-tided tide-gauge residuals, then thin to
the kind of cadence (3 min) we would actually use.

| Gauge | Location | Lat, Lon | Cell | Depth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **G1** | Brisbane Bar | $-27.37°S$, $153.17°E$ | (15, 54) | 6.0 m |
| **G2** | Wellington Point | $-27.48°S$, $153.24°E$ | (22, 42) | 6.0 m |
| **G3** | Tangalooma Roads | $-27.21°S$, $153.32°E$ | (30, 72) | 6.4 m |
| **G4** | Russell Channel | $-27.66°S$, $153.35°E$ | (33, 22) | 6.0 m |

These four timeseries plus the bathymetry and physics are all the
information the inverse solver gets to work with. The river-mouth
source $\psi(t)$ is *hidden*.

### The inverse problem, two ways {#sec-inverse}

We try two complementary approaches that bracket the spectrum
covered by the rest of the course.

**Method A — Naive PINN.** Train a smooth MLP $\eta_\theta(x, y, t)$
on inputs scaled to $[-1, 1]^3$ to match the gauge observations,
satisfy the wave equation (@eq-wave-eta) at random collocation
points, and respect the zero initial condition. Treat the recovered
source as $\psi_\theta(t) := \eta_\theta(x_r, y_r, t)$. This is what
[de Wolff et al. (2021)](../references/references.qmd#ref-dewolff2021){target="_blank"}
classify as the "vanilla PINN" baseline and what
[§7.2](../unit_07/unit_07.qmd) of this course re-derives in detail.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# Pseudocode for the naive-PINN loss (see scripts/train_inverse_pinn.jl)
function total_loss(θ, Xphys, Kx, Ky, Xz, Xt, Xsm)
    # Data: gauge readings ↔ η_θ at the gauge cells
    L_data = mean((η_batch(GAUGE_INPUT, θ) .- GAUGE_TARGET).^2)

    # Physics: ∂_ττ η  =  K_x ∂_ξξ η + K_y ∂_ζζ η  in normalised coords,
    #   sampled at random water-cell collocation points (excluding a
    #   small radius around the Dirichlet source).
    η_p = reshape(η_batch(Xphys, θ), 7, :)
    η_ξξ = (η_p[2, :] .- 2 .* η_p[1, :] .+ η_p[3, :]) ./ H_NX^2
    η_ζζ = (η_p[4, :] .- 2 .* η_p[1, :] .+ η_p[5, :]) ./ H_NY^2
    η_ττ = (η_p[6, :] .- 2 .* η_p[1, :] .+ η_p[7, :]) ./ H_NT^2
    L_phys = mean((η_ττ .- Kx .* η_ξξ .- Ky .* η_ζζ) .^ 2)

    # IC: η_θ(·, ·, 0) ≈ 0  and  ∂_t η_θ(·, ·, 0) ≈ 0
    # Smoothness: ψ_θ(t) = η_θ(x_r, y_r, t) gently regularised
    # ... see the script for the IC and smoothness terms
    return LAM_DATA*L_data + LAM_PHYS*L_phys + LAM_IC*L_ic + ...
end
```

**Method B — Adjoint inverse using the simulator as a forward map.**
Because the linearised SWE is *linear* in $\psi$, the forward map
$G: \psi(\cdot) \mapsto \eta_g(\cdot)$ is a linear operator. Compute
its impulse response once (a single FD pass with a narrow Gaussian
pulse), assemble $G$ as a Toeplitz convolution matrix, and solve the
Tikhonov-regularised linear least-squares problem

$$
\hat\psi \;=\; \arg\min_\psi \;
\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|G\psi - g_{\text{obs}}\|_2^2
\;+\; \tfrac{\lambda^2}{2}\,\|\mathrm{L}^{(2)} \psi\|_2^2,
$$

where $\mathrm{L}^{(2)}$ is the discrete second-difference operator
(a smoothness prior on $\psi$). No neural network — but it uses the
same physics that the PINN tries to learn.

```{julia}
#| eval: false
# Pseudocode for the adjoint inverse (scripts/train_inverse_adjoint.jl)
h_g = fd_forward(narrow_gaussian_pulse)            # impulse response per gauge
G   = vcat([toeplitz_from_impulse(h_g[:, k]) for k in 1:NG]...)
A   = vcat(G, λ_smooth * L2, λ_anchor * e1')      # stacked LHS
b   = vcat(g_obs, zeros(size(L2, 1)), 0.0)
ψ̂   = A \ b                                       # closed-form Tikhonov
```

### What we recover

![Top: the true ψ(t) (red) vs the adjoint inverse (blue, using the SWE
solver as forward map) vs the naive PINN (orange dashed, smooth-MLP
η-network with ψ read at the source cell). Middle / bottom: predicted
gauge timeseries at G1 (Brisbane Bar) and G2 (Wellington Point)
overlaid on the noisy observations both methods see.](figures/inverse_recovery.png)

The plot is the centrepiece of Unit 1. Two observations matter
pedagogically:

1. **Both methods fit the gauge observations.** Look at the G1 / G2
   panels: the adjoint prediction (blue) and the naive-PINN
   prediction (dashed orange) both lie comfortably inside the noisy
   cloud of observations. By the metric the algorithms are
   optimising, both succeed equally well.
2. **They disagree wildly on what produced those gauges.** The
   adjoint inverse recovers both surge peaks at roughly correct
   amplitude. The naive PINN gets the *timing* of the main pulse
   but flattens its amplitude to $\sim 0.14\,\text{m}$ — a factor
   of three under.

This is the classic signature of an **ill-posed inverse problem**:
many qualitatively different sources can produce the same downstream
signal once it has been spread by the physics, smoothed by the
gauges, and contaminated by noise. The remedy is to add a *prior* —
the adjoint inverse adds it explicitly through Tikhonov smoothness;
the naive PINN implicitly priors-in the smooth-MLP ansatz, which
turns out to bias the answer in the wrong direction here.

[de Wolff et al. (2021)](../references/references.qmd#ref-dewolff2021){target="_blank"}
documented exactly this failure mode on the same linearised SWE
problem.
[§7.2–§7.3](../unit_07/unit_07.qmd#sec-modern-fixes) walk through
the modern fixes — Fourier feature embeddings, causal training,
hard boundary-condition enforcement, adaptive loss weighting —
that close the gap.

## 1.3 The capstone preview: an AIMS thermistor column

The Moreton Bay surge is a 2-D *shallow-water* problem. The capstone
across Units 8–10 keeps the inverse-problem flavour but moves the
physics: a **1-D vertical column of ocean** at three AIMS-monitored
reef sites along the central Great Barrier Reef, with **a
thermistor chain** sampling temperature at five depths every hour.

After a storm passes through, the deeper sensors record an
unexpected cooling pattern. The competing hypotheses:

1. The storm intensified **upwelling** — cold water pumped up from depth.
2. The storm enhanced **vertical mixing** — heat drawn down from the surface faster than usual.
3. **Surface heating reduced** — cloud cover and evaporation cut the net flux into the ocean.

Each leaves a distinct fingerprint in the depth–time record. By
[Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) we build a PINN that, given the
mooring data, identifies which mechanism dominated. The full model
specification lives in [Unit 10](../unit_10/unit_10.qmd).

Same intellectual shape as today's worked example — *physics +
sparse data → unknown driver* — but with a different geometry,
different physics, and a richer inverse-problem story.

## 1.4 Course roadmap

[Unit 2](../unit_02/unit_02.qmd) covers machine-learning basics and
deep learning — the function-approximation toolkit.
[Unit 3](../unit_03/unit_03.qmd) surveys the broader Sci-ML and
physics-informed ML landscape.
[Unit 4](../unit_04/unit_04.qmd) introduces ODEs through universal
approximation (Neural ODEs, UDEs).
[Unit 5](../unit_05/unit_05.qmd) is your first PINN, on basic ODE
and PDE models.
[Unit 6](../unit_06/unit_06.qmd) covers formal PDE theory and
classical numerics.
[Unit 7](../unit_07/unit_07.qmd) covers modern PINN techniques for
harder PDEs — including the exact failure mode we just saw on the
naive PINN.
[Unit 8](../unit_08/unit_08.qmd) builds the full forward column +
shallow-water capstone model.
[Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) closes the loop by recovering an
unknown driver from sparse mooring data.

### 75 % Julia, 25 % Python

Julia is the primary language: `Lux.jl`, `NeuralPDE.jl`,
`MethodOfLines.jl`, the broader SciML stack. Python parallels appear
in [Unit 2](../unit_02/unit_02.qmd) (`scikit-learn`, `PyTorch`) and
[Unit 9](../unit_09/unit_09.qmd) (`DeepXDE`) so participants leave
with a sense of the cross-ecosystem landscape.
